description: Let's create the best Lunar Landing Site Navigator ever.
summary: Protocol Lunaris is an educational decision-support tool that answers a question mission planners face every time a lunar launch slips: if we land a week later, or at a nearby site, will we still have sunlight and a direct line of sight to Earth? Users pick a landing date and mission length (1 to 28 days) and the tool checks 14 lunar sites: a sample point in each of the nine south pole regions NASA selected in 2024 for the first crewed landing, the IM-2 CLPS site, the Shackleton-de Gerlache ridge, Apollo 11, Chandrayaan-3 and Chang'e-4. For each site it shows where the Sun and Earth sit against the real horizon, how many hours each stays visible, the longest stretch without each, and whether the site meets three example requirements. One click delays the landing by 7 days. Sun and Earth positions come from NASA/JPL Horizons; at the south pole the horizon is computed from LRO LOLA laser-altimetry topography, which changes the answer completely. It turns detailed NASA data into a fast, visual comparison for engineers, educators and the public.
details:
Project Details

WHAT IT DOES

Missions to the lunar south pole live on the edge: the Sun stays within a few degrees of the horizon and Earth rises and sets as the Moon wobbles (libration). A hill a few degrees high can hide the Sun for days. When a launch slips, teams must quickly check whether a new date or a nearby site still works. The tools that hold this information (JPL Horizons, QuickMap, Moon Trek) are powerful but slow for quick "what if" comparisons. Protocol Lunaris puts the answer on two screens:

  • Map screen. A south pole map built from LOLA topography shows the 11 south pole sites and the outlines of the nine candidate regions NASA selected in October 2024 for the first crewed landing (then planned as Artemis III; NASA now plans that landing as Artemis IV, in 2028). A "Whole Moon" map shows Apollo 11, Chandrayaan-3 and Chang'e-4. The user picks a landing date (UTC) and a duration, presses ANALYZE, and gets every site ranked: green if it meets all requirements, red if not, with the hours of the mission when the Sun and Earth are visible at the same time. A short list of recommended dates shows when the most sites work.
  • Horizon screen. For one site: the terrain silhouette around it, with the Sun and Earth and their paths during the mission; a timeline with Sun, Earth and "both" visibility bands that can be played or dragged; at the cursor, the elevation and azimuth of each body, how far it is above or below the terrain, and when it next rises or sets; for the whole mission, the visible hours, the longest gap without each body, and whether each requirement is met. A "+7d" button delays the landing by a week.
  • About and Sources. Each site has its context and facts computed from the data. A Sources window lists every dataset, the model, its simplifications and the use of AI.

The three example requirements are our team's demonstration assumptions, not NASA criteria: at most 48 h without the Sun, at most 72 h without Earth, and the Sun and Earth visible together at least 60% of the mission. A failed requirement is never compensated by a good indicator, so every result is explainable.

WHY IT MATTERS

The data shows how fragile south pole missions are. For a 14-day mission landing on 14 Dec 2026, 10 of the 11 south pole sites meet the requirements; delay the landing by 7 days and none do. Over the whole year, for 210 of the 351 possible landing dates no south pole site meets them for a 14-day mission. No site meets them for missions of 29 days or longer, so the tool caps missions at 28 days and explains why. Terrain matters as much as the date: on the Shackleton-de Gerlache ridge a flat 0° horizon would mean 165 days in a row without sunlight, while the real terrain seen from 2 m up gives a longest night of 12 days and sunlight 86% of the year. At the IM-2 site the opposite happens: nearby high ground cuts sunlight from 52% to 46% of the year.

For planners this is a fast first look before detailed analysis. For students and the public it shows, with real NASA data, why landing at the lunar south pole is so hard.

HOW IT WORKS

  • Ephemeris. A Python pipeline queries the NASA/JPL Horizons API (DE441) for the apparent azimuth and elevation of the Sun and Earth seen from each site, every hour for one year (14 Nov 2026 to 14 Nov 2027), with no atmospheric refraction. Horizons includes lunar libration. Results become visibility windows, so the app needs no internet connection and loads instantly.
  • Real terrain horizon. For the 11 south pole sites we compute the true horizon in 1,440 directions (every 0.25°), combining LOLA elevation maps at 5 m, 20 m and 80 m per pixel with exact 3D geometry on the lunar sphere, so the Moon's curvature is included. A body counts as visible when its center is above the terrain in its direction, for an observer 2 m above the ground.
  • Candidate regions. NASA publishes regions, not landing points. We use the official outlines (USGS data release based on LROC QuickMap) and place one sample point in each with a fixed rule: the best-lit 3x3-pixel block in NASA's LOLA average illumination map, then the highest ground inside it. These are sample points for comparison, not landing sites.
  • Validation. Our 86% sunlight for the ridge, seen from 2 m, falls inside the 77.1-88.0% range Glaser et al. (2018) report at 2 m for the best-lit polar sites, with the maximum on this same ridge. For all 11 south pole sites we also recompute the result the way NASA's LOLA illumination and Earth visibility maps define it (Mazarico et al. 2011): every site falls within the range of the map's neighboring pixels, with a mean absolute difference of 4.5 percentage points for the Sun and 2.7 for Earth. Periods and resolutions differ, so this shows consistency, not equality. Automated tests check every number in the app against reference values computed in Python (503 checks).
  • Interface. A Godot 4 app (GDScript) in pixel-art style, in English, Portuguese and Spanish. It only reads the prepared data files and adds up the visibility windows for the chosen mission; it never invents or extrapolates values, and dates outside the data show "Insufficient data".

LIMITATIONS

  • Hourly data: times are shown to the hour, in UTC.
  • Visibility uses the center of the Sun or Earth.
  • Real terrain is computed for the 11 south pole sites; the other three use a flat 0° horizon, and the screen says so.
  • Each candidate region is represented by one sample point; conditions vary a lot inside a region.
  • No solar panel, battery, antenna or radio link model: the tool reports sunlight hours and geometric Earth visibility, not power or guaranteed communication.
  • Educational tool; it does not certify landing sites.

TOOLS

Python (standard library, NumPy, Pillow, Matplotlib) for the data pipeline, terrain horizons and validation; Godot Engine 4.7 with GDScript for the interface. AI coding assistance (Claude, by Anthropic) was used for parts of the data-processing code, the Godot interface code and the Portuguese and Spanish translations, following the team's specification and reviewed by the team. Every number on screen comes from NASA data and fixed rules, not from generative AI.
